transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-19 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~49 minutes
Attendees: Avery Cole (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Head of ML - LinguaCorp), Evan Brooks (Eng Mgr), Priya Nair (Security/SRE), Tom (Product)

Summary:
High-level discovery for an integration pilot: LinguaCorp wants to evaluate Redwood for a translation-assist product that needs low-latency token streaming, observability into per-request cost, and a private deployment option for certain enterprise customers. They asked about SDKs, LangChain / LlamaIndex support, gateway/proxy patterns, rate limiting/quotas, VPC/private deployment, and audit/KMS requirements. Team agreed on a short pilot: 2-week bench + security review.

Topics covered:
- SDKs and quickstart, LangChain & LlamaIndex connectors
- Gateway/proxy architecture and edge caching
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs (latency, cost, data residency)
- Rate limits, per-route quotas, burst handling
- Observability hooks: traces, token-level cost, export to their Datadog/Prometheus
- Security: SOC2, SSO, KMS, VPC peering, on-prem option

Transcript body (timestamps are approximate, speaker attribution sometimes noisy):
[00:00] Avery: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll run for about 45 minutes, quick intros and then dive into your integration constraints.
[00:08] Maya: hi i'm Maya, head of ML, we own the translator models and the inference pipeline for LinguaCorp.
[00:12] Evan: Evan here, engineering manager for the product team.
[00:15] Priya: Priya, security and SRE.
[00:18] Diego: Diego, solutions engineer at Redwood. I'll do the technical walkthrough.
[00:22] Tom: Tom, product, quick clarifying q's on UX.
[00:25] Avery: cool. quick context from us: Redwood's runtime supports streaming, token-level cost breakdowns, dedicated capacity and private deployment with VPC/options if you need on-prem. we'll focus on the parts you called out: sdk, gateway/proxy, quotas, and observability.
[00:39] Maya: our main constraint is latency for interactive translation -- p95 needs to be under 400ms for short request paths. some enterprise customers require data never leave their VPC. how do you handle that?
[00:49] Diego: right, so two main options: Hosted with private endpoints and strict retention policies, or Redwood Private which installs a control plane in your VPC and inference plane on your infrastructure. Hosted gives faster onboarding, Dedicated in our cloud gives predictable throughput, Private is full VPC/onprem for data residency.
[01:10] Maya: and for the private option what's the onboarding time? our security team is very time-constrained.
[01:14] Diego: typical private on‑ramp is 4–8 weeks depending on KMS integration and networking. if you can accept a VPC peering setup with our private control plane it's often faster — like 2–3 weeks. full air‑gapped on‑prem can be longer.
[01:30] Priya: do you support customer-managed KMS/HSM? we need key separation.
[01:34] Avery: yes, we integrate with customer KMS like AWS KMS and can reference customer keys for model artifacts and logs; HSM options available for Private. we also provide audit logs.
[01:44] Evan: on the SDK side, we've got a lot of code that depends on LangChain and LlamaIndex. are there first-class connectors or examples?
[01:50] Diego: yes, we maintain SDKs in Python, Node; there are LangChain and LlamaIndex community connectors and an official example repo. you'll be able to use Redwood model endpoints as a LangChain llm wrapper or a LlamaIndex service connector. we also have streaming token hooks for LangChain agents.
[02:08] Maya: ok, are there known issues with async streaming and LangChain agents? last time we tried a provider we saw token interleaving and partial failures.
[02:16] Diego: there's a nuance: streaming semantics depend on the SDK version and how you wire the callback threads. our SDK exposes an 'incremental' callback with ordering guarantees; if you're using older LangChain code there can be mismatches. we can share a patch and a sample agent wiring.
[02:34] Tom: regarding gateway/proxy — our infra uses an internal gateway that routes requests to multiple LLM endpoints and handles auth. do you recommend a direct SDK integration in the service or putting Redwood behind our gateway?
[02:45] Diego: both are valid. putting Redwood behind your gateway is common — treat Redwood like any external model endpoint. but consider using our client-side SDK and a short-lived token to reduce load on your gateway for token streaming. for caching common prompts we recommend prefix caching at the gateway edge, and using Redwood's KV cache for recurrent conversation state.
[03:08] Maya: KV cache as in kv, key‑value cache for context? we've seen the 'K-V cash' typo in some transcripts...
[03:14] Diego: yeah the KV cache — it stores recent key/value attention state to speed up autoregressive decoding. it helps when you have long histories and want to avoid re-computation.
[03:22] Evan: about quotas: we need per-tenant rate limits and burst handling. can Redwood enforce per-api-key quotas?
[03:29] Avery: yes, you can set per-token quotas and rate limits per API key or route. we support burst windows and can shape traffic; for Dedicated you can also reserve pool capacity with guaranteed throughput to avoid noisy neighbors.
[03:42] Priya: do you have throttling callbacks so our gateway can surface 429s back to the app gracefully?
[03:48] Diego: we include structured error payloads with X-Rate-Limit headers; you can wire them into your gateway. we also do proactive routing to lower-cost model variants if capacity is constrained.
[03:59] Maya: observability: we use Datadog and Prometheus. we need per-request traces, token counts, and cost labels.
[04:05] Diego: Redwood Console emits per-request metrics and can forward traces via OpenTelemetry. you can export token cost as tags, send traces to Datadog, and push metrics to Prometheus. we also support a webhooks export for per-request events if you want a custom pipeline.
[04:20] Evan: can we get the raw token timing (per-token latency) for debugging?
[04:24] Diego: yes, but note that per-token timing inside the GPU can be noisy; we provide an aggregated breakdown: request queuing, batching latency, compilation time, and per-token decode times. for benching we'll give p50/p95/p99.
[04:38] Priya: one security thing — we need to see how audit logs store prompts. can you redact pii and configure retention windows?
[04:45] Avery: audit logs can be configured with redaction and retention policies. for Private you can keep logs inside your VPC and integrate with your SIEM. for Hosted we offer short retention and redaction options, but some enterprise customers choose Private to ensure full control.
[04:58] Tom: curious about model fallback behavior — if you hit capacity, what's your recommended approach?
[05:03] Diego: we support automated fallback policies: route to cheaper quantized variants, fall back to lower-latency smaller models, or queue with a priority service. policies are configurable per-route.
[05:17] Maya: economics are key. for high-volume transient traffic, can we do dedicated bursts?
[05:23] Avery: Dedicated supports burst capacity and autoscaling policies. you can reserve baseline GPUs and allow bursts to a larger pool. billing differentiates reserved capacity vs overage. we'll share sample math in the pricing doc.
[05:36] Evan: on integration complexity — what does the quickstart look like? how long to get a PoC up?
[05:42] Diego: with Hosted you can be calling a test model in under an hour via the SDK or REST. for a realistic PoC with streaming and gateway integration, plan 1–2 weeks. Dedicated is a few weeks. Private ranges 2–8 weeks depending on networking.
[05:58] Priya: do you require any ports open for VPC peering? we need specifics for our firewall team.
[06:03] Diego: we'll provide a network topology doc. for peering we use standard HTTPS/TLS endpoints and optional peering for control plane calls. Private installs may require extra ports for gRPC internal comms; we'll provide exact port lists.
[06:18] Maya: a few technical dive questions — we rely heavily on LangChain chains invoking tools and retrieval. how do you suggest integrating retrieval augmented generation (RAG) with LlamaIndex on top of Redwood?
[06:28] Diego: typical setup: you keep your vector DB (we see Pinecone/Weaviate/FAISS) behind your gateway, retrieval returns docs to the app layer which builds a prompt; you call Redwood for generation. LlamaIndex connectors can orchestrate retrieval and send chunks to Redwood. For latency-sensitive flows, prefetch and warm KV cache or use smaller context windows plus caching on the gateway.
[06:49] Tom: any sample repos for RAG + LlamaIndex?
[06:52] Diego: yes, we'll link a repo with a LangChain agent + LlamaIndex pipeline integrated with Redwood streaming and a gateway pattern.
[06:58] Maya: in terms of SDK features, does your node sdk support streaming and abort semantics?
[07:03] Diego: yes, Node SDK supports streaming and an abort controller. Python has async generators. streaming events include token, delta, and final events. abort will attempt a graceful stop, but depending on model and network you may see some trailing tokens.
[07:18] Evan: we'd like to test token-level cost attribution for multi-tenant requests. can you return per-tenant cost in response metadata?
[07:24] Avery: we can attach cost tags and per-request cost summaries. for multi-tenant setups we recommend using per-tenant API keys and billing aggregations in Console.
[07:35] Priya: compliance: do you provide SOC2 reports? ISO?
[07:38] Avery: yes, we have SOC2 Type II and are pursuing ISO 27001; we can share our compliance pack in an NDA'd share. Private customers can keep logs in their environment which helps with audits.
[07:49] Maya: one more thing — some of our customers require on-prem inference for PII-heavy data. how frictioned is the on‑prem package?
[07:56] Diego: on-prem is available as a packaged runtime plus installer; it supports local GPUs and model artifacts. onboarding is heavier because we need to validate infra, licensing, and often do an OLA for hardware. typical timeline 6–8 weeks.
[08:10] Tom: for the pilot we'd like a sandbox with sample small model and streaming enabled so product can prototype. what's the minimum footprint?
[08:16] Diego: you can start with a single small GPU instance (A100/RTX) for dev. Hosted sandbox is easiest: we'll provide API keys scoped to a sandbox org and example prompts.
[08:28] Maya: sounds good. question about retries — if a generation fails mid-stream do you support resume or do we have to restart?
[08:35] Diego: we don't have token-level resume for arbitrary models; we support re-try semantics at the request level and can attempt to re-decode from cached KV states for recent contexts. resumable streams are something on the roadmap but not universally supported.
[08:52] Evan: ok. another operational q: we want to correlate app request id with Redwood traces for debugging. can we inject an x-request-id that appears in Console/traces?
[08:59] Diego: yes add x-request-id header and it will surface in logs/traces so you can correlate with your APM.
[09:05] Priya: network encryption in transit and at rest?
[09:08] Avery: TLS 1.2+ in transit, data at rest encrypted using customer-managed keys where available. Private can be fully inside your VPC.
[09:17] Maya: what's the retry/backoff pattern you recommend for clients?
[09:20] Diego: exponential backoff with jitter, but for streaming flows consider short circuiting if you catch a specific 429 that indicates capacity; if it's a transient network issue retry, but don't retry streaming partial sessions.
[09:35] Tom: can we do a canary routing? e.g., route 5% of traffic to Redwood and 95% to incumbent?
[09:40] Avery: yes, we support route-based rollouts and canary percentages in the Console. you can also set model pins and fallback policies per-route.
[09:50] Maya: excellent. let's talk timeline: we'd like a 2-week bench + pilot to evaluate latency and economics before Q3 procurement.
[09:58] Avery: sounds doable. proposal: 2-week benchmarking pilot using your sample prompts. Redwood provides sandbox keys, Diego runs a bench and shares p95/p99 plus cost estimates. Security pack shared to Priya.
[10:12] Priya: i want a network diagram and list of required IPs/ports, plus clarifying retention for logs.
[10:18] Avery: we'll include that in the security pack.
[10:21] Evan: are there any gotchas with LangChain rate-limiting while using callbacks?
[10:25] Diego: one gotcha is if the LangChain agent triggers many parallel invocations, you can accidentally blow per-key quotas. recommend client-side pooling or a queue in the gateway. also watch for concurrency in async generators.
[10:39] Maya: if we do Dedicated, how do we handle model updates and rollouts? do you support canary model versions?
[10:45] Diego: yes, rollouts are supported. you can pin a route to a model version, do canaries, and set automatic fallback to previous stable version. we also have rollbacks and traffic shifting.
[10:56] Tom: what's the telemetry retention in Console default?
[10:59] Avery: default retention is 30 days for detailed traces, longer for aggregated metrics. enterprise tiers can increase retention.
[11:07] Priya: are we able to revoke keys quickly if an issue happens?
[11:10] Diego: yes, we provide immediate key revocation and session invalidation.
[11:14] Maya: great. ok recap of agreed pilot steps?
[11:17] Avery: summary: Redwood to provide sandbox org + API keys, security pack (SOC2, network topology, KMS details), pricing matrix; Diego runs 48hr bench using LinguaCorp prompts and returns latency/cost breakdown; LinguaCorp to review results and schedule a security follow-up.
[11:34] Tom: timeline for bench results?
[11:36] Diego: i'll have results within 48 hours of spinup, target by 2026-05-22.
[11:41] Priya: security meeting week of 2026-05-25 works.
[11:44] Avery: i'll send the SOW and pricing by 2026-05-21.
[11:48] Maya: thanks everyone.
[11:50] Avery: thanks all, we'll follow up in writing.
[11:55] -- end --
